---
url: https://reqsign.apache.org/docs/guides/upgrading-to-0.21/
---
# Upgrading to Reqsign 0.21 | Apache Reqsign™

# Upgrading to Reqsign 0.21

0.21 moves the core and every established service crate to one new lockstep major (`4.0.0`), publishes the provider crates added since 0.20.8, and removes cryptographic implementations from the signing crates. Most applications need three steps:

1. Update the facade to `0.21` and let it pull the matching `4.0.0` components.
2. Make sure the `Context` handed to a signer can resolve a `CryptoProvider`.
3. Pass the `Context` explicitly to `default_signer`.

Everything else on this page is the detail behind those steps.

## Dependency versions[​](#dependency-versions "Direct link to Dependency versions")

| Crate                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | 0.20 line | 0.21 line |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | --------- |
| reqsign                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | 0.20.x    | 0.21.x    |
| reqsign-core, reqsign-aws-core, every established service crate, reqsign-file-read-tokio, reqsign-command-execute-tokio                                                                                                                             | 3.x       | 4.0.0     |
| reqsign-http-send-reqwest                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | 4.0.x     | 5.0.0     |
| reqsign-crypto-rustcrypto, reqsign-crypto-boring                                                                                                                                                                                                    | —         | 1.0.0     |
| reqsign-aliyun-drive, reqsign-baidu-netdisk, reqsign-cloudflare, reqsign-dropbox, reqsign-github, reqsign-koofr, reqsign-oauth2, reqsign-onedrive, reqsign-seafile, reqsign-upyun, reqsign-vercel, reqsign-yandex-disk, and the B2 crate reqsign-b2 | —         | 1.0.0     |

Mixing core majors does not compile, because the traits are the compatibility boundary. Upgrade the facade and every directly used `reqsign-*` crate in the same change:

```

[dependencies]

reqsign = "0.21"


# Only if you use these crates directly:

reqsign-core = "4"

reqsign-aws-v4 = "4"

reqsign-http-send-reqwest = "5"


```

## Cryptography now comes from the context[​](#cryptography-now-comes-from-the-context "Direct link to Cryptography now comes from the context")

Reqsign no longer links SHA-1, SHA-256, HMAC, RSA, P-256, or AES-GCM into`reqsign-core` or any service crate. Signing resolves a`reqsign_core::crypto::CryptoProvider` through the `Context`, in this order:

1. `Context::with_crypto(provider)` — explicit binding, highest priority.
2. `reqsign_core::crypto::install_default(provider)` — process-wide registration.
3. Otherwise `ErrorKind::ConfigInvalid` at the point of use.

`Context::new()` and `Context::default()` start unbound. Signing with an unbound context fails instead of silently using a bundled implementation.

### Facade users[​](#facade-users "Direct link to Facade users")

`default_context()` keeps working. With the `default-crypto` feature, which is part of `default`, it binds `RustCryptoProvider` when the process-wide slot is empty; it never installs the global provider itself. No startup boilerplate is required:

```

use reqsign::{aws, default_context};


let ctx = default_context();

let signer = aws::default_signer(ctx, "s3", "us-east-1");


```

To choose a single backend for the whole application, install it before constructing contexts. Contexts that already bound RustCrypto keep that binding; explicit `with_crypto` always wins:

```

use reqsign::RustCryptoProvider;


// Returns Err when another component already installed a provider.

RustCryptoProvider::install_default()

    .map_err(|_| "a CryptoProvider is already installed")?;


```

Middleware and libraries should not install a global provider. They should accept the caller's `Context` instead.

### Bare `reqsign-core` users[​](#bare-reqsign-core-users "Direct link to bare-reqsign-core-users")

```

use reqsign_core::{Context, OsEnv, Signer};

use reqsign_crypto_rustcrypto::RustCryptoProvider;


let ctx = Context::new()

    .with_crypto(RustCryptoProvider::new())

    .with_env(OsEnv);


```

### Custom providers[​](#custom-providers "Direct link to Custom providers")

Implement `reqsign_core::crypto::CryptoProvider`. `sha1`, `sha256`,`hmac_sha1`, and `hmac_sha256` are mandatory; the remaining operations have default implementations that return `ConfigInvalid` so a minimal provider can serve the services that only need hashing and MACs.

A provider or operation that is missing is a non-retryable `ConfigInvalid`. Malformed key material is `CredentialInvalid`. Backend failures are`Unexpected`.

The generic credential chain continues past provider errors and returns`Ok(None)` when every source is exhausted, so a missing provider discovered while loading credentials can surface as `CredentialInvalid` from`Signer::sign` with the request unchanged. Bind or install a provider before loading credentials to see the `ConfigInvalid` failure itself.

### Removed and changed crypto APIs[​](#removed-and-changed-crypto-apis "Direct link to Removed and changed crypto APIs")

* The public `reqsign_core::jwt` module and the `jwt` feature are removed. Azure client-certificate and Google service-account flows format RS256 JWS internally through the resolved provider. Callers that used `reqsign_core::jwt`must call `CryptoProvider::rsa_pkcs1v15_sha256_sign` and format the JWS themselves.
* Hash and MAC helpers take a provider and return `Result`:  
```  
// 0.20  
let digest = reqsign_core::hash::hex_sha256(body);  
// 0.21  
let digest = reqsign_core::hash::hex_sha256(ctx.crypto_provider()?, body)?;  
```
* Azure `ServiceSharedAccessSignature::token` takes the resolved provider:`sas.token(ctx.crypto_provider()?)?`.
* Base64 helpers (`base64_encode`, `base64_decode`) are unchanged.

### Backend crates[​](#backend-crates "Direct link to Backend crates")

* `reqsign-crypto-rustcrypto` implements all operations and supports`wasm32-unknown-unknown` for SHA-1, SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-1/256, and P-256 ECDSA. RSA, AES-GCM, and random generation report `ConfigInvalid` there.
* `reqsign-crypto-boring` is native-only, excluded from the main workspace, and forwards an optional `fips` feature. Bind it explicitly:`Context::new().with_crypto(BoringCryptoProvider::new())`.

## Default signers take an explicit `Context`[​](#default-signers-take-an-explicit-context "Direct link to default-signers-take-an-explicit-context")

Every per-service `default_signer` now takes the context as its first argument. The `default-context` feature no longer gates `DefaultSigner` or`default_signer`: they exist whenever the service feature is enabled, including custom-runtime and WASM builds.

```

// 0.20

let signer = reqsign::aws::default_signer("s3", "us-east-1");

let signer = reqsign::azure::default_signer();


// 0.21

let ctx = reqsign::default_context();

let signer = reqsign::aws::default_signer(ctx.clone(), "s3", "us-east-1");

let signer = reqsign::azure::default_signer(ctx);


```

Passing one shared context lets several signers and granters reuse the same HTTP client and credential adapters instead of building a new runtime per call.

## Replacing a signer's `Context` starts an empty credential cache[​](#replacing-a-signers-context-starts-an-empty-credential-cache "Direct link to replacing-a-signers-context-starts-an-empty-credential-cache")

A silent cache miss, not a compile error

`Signer::with_context` now gives the returned signer a new, empty credential cache. In 0.20 it kept the previous cache; in 0.21 the next `sign` has to load a credential again. Code that replaces the context per request still compiles, but each request's signer starts empty and repeats the provider's work, such as IMDS or STS calls, OAuth 2.0 or Entra ID token requests, or reads of local credential files.

This isolation is intentional. A `Context` carries `Env`, `FileRead`,`CommandExecute`, and `HttpSend`, so replacing it can change which identity or endpoint a provider resolves. Reusing the previous cache could sign with a credential that belongs to a different identity. Each signer owns its cache, and replacing the context replaces that cache as well.

The common regression is replacing the context inside the request path, often to inject a per-operation HTTP transport:

```

// Compiles, but each request starts with an empty cache and reloads.

let signer = self

    .signer

    .clone()

    .with_context(self.ctx.clone().with_http_send(transport.clone()));

signer.sign(&mut parts, expires_in).await?;


```

Bind the context and build the signer once, when the client or connection scope is created:

```

let signer = Signer::new(

    ctx.with_http_send(transport),

    provider,

    request_signer,

);


// Then reuse that signer for every request in the same scope. Clones share

// its context and credential cache.

signer.sign(&mut parts, expires_in).await?;


```

If the application has several stable transports or credential scopes, keep one signer for each and reuse it, for example in a map keyed by transport or scope. Replace the context when the identity or transport genuinely changes, not on every request just to inject the current transport.

The other builders follow the same cache boundary:

* `with_request_signer` replaces only the signing operation and keeps the context, provider, and cached credential.
* `with_credential_provider` and `with_context` both start an empty cache, because either can change the credential or the identity that resolves it.
* `Signer::new` and `default_signer` also start with an empty cache. Construct them once per stable credential scope instead of once per request.
* For `Granter`, `with_credential_granter` keeps the cached source credential, while `with_context` and `with_credential_provider` start an empty cache.

When the provider returns static credentials or caches them itself, the repeated load can be cheap. That is a provider property, not a guarantee from`Signer`.

## Minimum supported Rust version is 1.87[​](#minimum-supported-rust-version-is-187 "Direct link to Minimum supported Rust version is 1.87")

The RustCrypto backend's `rsa 0.10` dependency requires Rust 1.87, and the workspace declares `rust-version = "1.87.0"`. Builds on Rust 1.86 fail during dependency resolution.

## New provider crates[​](#new-provider-crates "Direct link to New provider crates")

These crates and facade features are published for the first time at `1.0.0`. They depend on `reqsign-core` 4 and follow the same `Context` and signing contracts as the established services:

| Facade feature | Crate                 | Scope                                                |
| -------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| aliyun-drive   | reqsign-aliyun-drive  | Aliyun Drive Open Platform OAuth and bearer signing  |
| b2             | reqsign-b2            | Backblaze B2 Native API                              |
| baidu-netdisk  | reqsign-baidu-netdisk | Baidu Netdisk static access-token query signing      |
| cloudflare     | reqsign-cloudflare    | Cloudflare API token requests (KV, D1)               |
| dropbox        | reqsign-dropbox       | Dropbox OAuth 2.0 bearer authentication              |
| github         | reqsign-github        | GitHub.com bearer tokens and anonymous public access |
| koofr          | reqsign-koofr         | Koofr access-token exchange and request signing      |
| oauth2         | reqsign-oauth2        | Shared OAuth 2.0 refresh grants                      |
| onedrive       | reqsign-onedrive      | Microsoft Graph OAuth 2.0 bearer authentication      |
| seafile        | reqsign-seafile       | Seafile account-token authentication                 |
| upyun          | reqsign-upyun         | UPYUN header signing                                 |
| vercel         | reqsign-vercel        | Vercel Blob and Artifacts bearer tokens              |
| yandex-disk    | reqsign-yandex-disk   | Yandex Disk OAuth credentials and signing            |

`reqsign-http-message-signatures` (RFC 9421, facade feature`http-message-signatures`) is also new; it joins the lockstep line and starts at`4.0.0` so it composes with `reqsign-core` 4.

Baidu Netdisk has no ambient credential source, so the caller supplies the token:

```

use reqsign::{baidu_netdisk, default_context};


let ctx = default_context();

let signer = baidu_netdisk::default_signer(ctx, access_token);


```

The caller still owns request policy, such as the `User-Agent` Baidu requires on download requests. Reqsign only signs the `access_token` query parameter and preserves the rest of the wire query.

## OBS and TOS credentials carry an absolute expiry[​](#obs-and-tos-credentials-carry-an-absolute-expiry "Direct link to OBS and TOS credentials carry an absolute expiry")

The Huawei Cloud OBS and Volcengine TOS `Credential` types gained`expires_at: Option<Timestamp>` in the v0.20.9 release-candidate source. That public field breaks struct-literal construction:

```

// 0.20 and earlier

let credential = obs::Credential {

    access_key_id,

    secret_access_key,

    security_token,

};


// 0.21, Huawei Cloud OBS: the constructor keeps the security token and leaves

// the expiration unset.

let credential = obs::Credential::new(access_key_id, secret_access_key, security_token)

    .with_expires_at(expires_at);


// 0.21, Volcengine TOS: the constructor takes only the key pair.

let credential = tos::Credential::new(&access_key_id, &secret_access_key)

    .with_session_token(&security_token)

    .with_expires_at(expires_at);


```

Header signing and presigning reject known-expiry credentials that do not cover the requested operation deadline; presigning checks the full lifetime of the signed URL. The STS granters (`AssumeRole` for TOS, IAM `Agency` for OBS) and Tencent COS `GetFederationToken` return credentials that carry the exact cloud-side expiration.

These changes already landed in the v0.20.9 release-candidate source, so they are new relative to the published 0.20.8 crates. If the v0.20.9 vote completes first, they reach crates.io there; the 0.21 release carries them either way.

## Behavior preserved[​](#behavior-preserved "Direct link to Behavior preserved")

Wire formats are unchanged: AWS SigV4/SigV4a, Azure Storage SAS/shared key/client certificate, Google signed URLs and CAB tokens, Oracle, Aliyun OSS, Huawei Cloud OBS, Tencent COS, and Volcengine TOS keep their canonicalization and encodings. `Signer::sign` is still atomic: on error, the request head is unchanged; on success, only the URI and headers may change.

url: https://reqsign.apache.org/docs/providers/aliyun-drive/

# Aliyun Drive | Apache Reqsign™

# Aliyun Drive

Aliyun Drive Open Platform API requests authenticated with an OAuth access token. The drive ID, file paths, upload URLs, request bodies, and storage API requests stay with the caller.

Bearer token✓ header signing— query / presign✓ WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-aliyun-drive ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-aliyun-drive)

Inserts a sensitive Authorization: Bearer header and leaves the URI and every other header unchanged; expires\_in is rejected because the service has no query authentication. The caller supplies the User-Agent required by the storage API.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features aliyun-drive

cargo add http@1


```

The default provider has no ambient source. Supply the identity explicitly:

```

use reqsign::{aliyun_drive, default_context};


let ctx = default_context();

let signer = aliyun_drive::default_signer(ctx)

    .with_credential_provider(aliyun_drive::StaticCredentialProvider::new("access-token"));


// The caller owns the drive ID, file path, and request body.

let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::POST)

    .uri("https://openapi.alipan.com/adrive/v1.0/openFile/get_by_path")

    .header(http::header::USER_AGENT, "my-application")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

## Credentials[​](#credentials "Direct link to Credentials")

Aliyun Drive Open Platform documents OAuth authorization and its token endpoint, but no CLI, SDK, environment-variable, or local-file credential discovery contract. Reqsign therefore does not invent an ambient source. Use`StaticCredentialProvider` for a caller-managed access token, or`RefreshCredentialProvider` for a confidential-client refresh token.

An explicit provider fails closed: an invalid token or refresh configuration returns an error instead of silently switching to a different identity.

### Refresh-token exchange[​](#refresh-token-exchange "Direct link to Refresh-token exchange")

Aliyun Drive uses OAuth 2.0 authorization but not the RFC 6749 form-encoded refresh request. The provider sends a vendor-specific JSON body:

```

POST https://openapi.alipan.com/oauth/access_token

Content-Type: application/json

User-Agent: reqsign-aliyun-drive/<version>


{"client_id":"...","client_secret":"...","grant_type":"refresh_token","refresh_token":"..."}


```

All three confidential-client credentials are required. Aliyun Drive's official PKCE public-client flow returns a 30-day access token without a refresh token, so public clients use `StaticCredentialProvider` with that access token, optionally with its absolute expiration. The endpoint requires a non-empty`User-Agent`. Use `with_token_endpoint` only to select another explicitly trusted HTTPS endpoint for the same confidential-client protocol.

A successful response returns `access_token`, `token_type`, `expires_in`, and a new single-use `refresh_token`. The provider keeps only the latest refresh token in memory. Clones share that state and exchanges are serialized, so concurrent callers use the latest rotated token. A successful, parseable response commits a non-empty rotated token even when the accompanying access token or expiry is unusable, because the previous refresh token was consumed. Tokens are never persisted, and Reqsign exposes no getter or persistence callback.`reqsign::Signer` owns access-token caching and refresh on expiry.

After a successful refresh, the initially configured refresh token may already have been consumed. Restarting with that original value can therefore fail. Restart with a fresh authorized grant, or let the application manage and persist its own refresh exchange and supply the resulting access token through`StaticCredentialProvider`.

```

use reqsign::{Signer, aliyun_drive, default_context};


let provider = aliyun_drive::RefreshCredentialProvider::new(

    "client-id",

    "client-secret",

    "refresh-token",

)?;

let signer = Signer::new(default_context(), provider, aliyun_drive::RequestSigner);


```

## Request behavior[​](#request-behavior "Direct link to Request behavior")

`RequestSigner` inserts a sensitive `Authorization: Bearer` header and leaves the URI and every other header unchanged. Drive IDs, file paths, upload URLs, request bodies, and the storage API requests stay with the caller. The service has no query authentication, so signing rejects `expires_in`.

The first-party storage API also requires a caller-supplied `User-Agent`; the signer does not add or replace it. The refresh request sets its own`User-Agent` because the token endpoint requires one.

The caller owns the HTTP client and its redirect policy. Do not forward the signed `Authorization` header to a different host.

## WASM[​](#wasm "Direct link to WASM")

Static credentials and header signing work on `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Refresh-token exchange works with a caller-provided HTTP adapter. On the`wasm-bindgen`\-hosted target, the crate enables Jiff's JavaScript clock so expiration checks can read time from the JS host.

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

This provider has no ambient default source. Supply an explicit credential provider as described on this page.

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-aliyun-drive/latest/reqsign%5Faliyun%5Fdrive/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static access token
* [RefreshCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-aliyun-drive/latest/reqsign%5Faliyun%5Fdrive/struct.RefreshCredentialProvider.html) — Confidential-client OAuth refresh token with a vendor JSON exchange

# AWS SigV4a | Apache Reqsign™

# AWS SigV4a

AWS services that accept Signature Version 4A for multi-region requests, addressed by service name and a region set (for example s3 with us-east-1,us-west-2).

AWS Signature Version 4A✓ header signing✓ query / presign✓ WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-aws-v4a ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-aws-v4a)

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

use reqsign::aws::v4a::{default_signer, SigningRegionSet};

// Same credential chain as SigV4; the signature covers a region set —

// built for multi-region endpoints like S3 Multi-Region Access Points.

let ctx = default_context();

let region_set = SigningRegionSet::new("us-east-1,us-west-2")?;

let signer = default_signer(ctx, "s3", region_set);


let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::GET)

    .uri("https://m1abcdefgh.mrap.accesspoint.s3-global.amazonaws.com/my-object")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;

# Backblaze B2 | Apache Reqsign™

# Backblaze B2

Backblaze B2 Native API requests authorized by an account authorization token. S3-compatible requests, bucket and file upload URL creation, download authorization, and storage operations remain the caller's responsibility.

B2 Native API account authorization token✓ header signing— query / presign✓ WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-b2 ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-b2)

Inserts the native account authorization token as a sensitive Authorization header. expires\_in raises the required credential validity but does not presign URLs; upload URL and download authorization calls stay with the caller.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features b2


```

```

use reqsign::{b2, default_context};


// B2_APPLICATION_KEY_ID and B2_APPLICATION_KEY — resolved by the default chain.

let ctx = default_context();

let signer = b2::default_signer(ctx);


let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::GET)

    .uri("https://api001.backblazeb2.com/b2api/v4/b2_list_buckets?accountId=account-id")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

The default chain exchanges `B2_APPLICATION_KEY_ID` and `B2_APPLICATION_KEY`for a Native API authorization token with the documented v4`b2_authorize_account` endpoint. The credential carries the authorization token, the Native API and download base URLs, and the earlier of the 24-hour token limit and the application key expiration timestamp. `Signer` caches and refreshes it.

The default source and prepended providers fail closed: a provider error is returned to the caller instead of falling through, so a retryable`b2_authorize_account` failure stays retryable.

Use `AccountAuthorizationCredentialProvider` for an explicit application key, or`StaticCredentialProvider` when the caller already obtained the token and base URLs. Key capabilities and bucket or prefix restrictions are enforced by B2 and remain server-side.

The signer covers Native API requests authorized by the account token. Creating upload URLs, requesting download authorization, and using the S3-compatible API remain the caller's responsibility.

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

The default signer tries these sources in order and uses the first one that yields a credential — no configuration needed when any of them is present:

1. B2\_APPLICATION\_KEY\_ID and B2\_APPLICATION\_KEY

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [EnvCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-b2/latest/reqsign%5Fb2/struct.EnvCredentialProvider.html) — B2\_APPLICATION\_KEY\_ID and B2\_APPLICATION\_KEY
* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-b2/latest/reqsign%5Fb2/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static authorization token and Native API endpoints
* [AccountAuthorizationCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-b2/latest/reqsign%5Fb2/struct.AccountAuthorizationCredentialProvider.html) — Explicit application key

url: https://reqsign.apache.org/docs/providers/baidu-netdisk/

# Baidu Netdisk | Apache Reqsign™

# Baidu Netdisk

Baidu Netdisk Open Platform xpan API requests authenticated with an access\_token query parameter; OAuth refresh, paths, storage operations, headers, and business requests remain caller-owned.

Baidu Netdisk access\_token query parameter— header signing✓ query / presign✓ WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-baidu-netdisk ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-baidu-netdisk)

Removes existing access\_token parameters and appends one form-encoded access\_token query parameter while preserving unrelated wire query bytes and all headers. expires\_in is rejected; OAuth refresh and persistence stay with the caller.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features baidu-netdisk


```

```

use reqsign::{baidu_netdisk, default_context};


// Supply the access token explicitly; Reqsign does not discover one.

let ctx = default_context();

let signer = baidu_netdisk::default_signer(ctx, "baidu-netdisk-access-token");


let mut req = http::Request::get(

    "https://pan.baidu.com/rest/2.0/xpan/file?method=list&dir=%2Fapps%2FMyApp",

)

.body(())?

.into_parts()

.0;


// Adds access_token=<token> to the query string.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

The [Baidu Netdisk Open Platform](https://pan.baidu.com/union/doc/) xpan APIs authenticate requests with an `access_token` query parameter. The signer removes any existing `access_token` parameter and appends one form-encoded parameter, so signing the same request again does not leave stale authentication. Existing percent escapes, parameter order, duplicate keys, empty values, literal `+` characters, and all headers are preserved.

## Credentials[​](#credentials "Direct link to Credentials")

`StaticCredentialProvider` accepts a token that the caller already obtained through Baidu's Open Platform authorization flow. Reqsign does not read an environment variable, a well-known credential file, or an OAuth token endpoint for Baidu Netdisk. OAuth refresh, single-use refresh-token rotation, and token persistence stay with the caller and are not implemented by this crate.

The token is a secret. `Debug` output for credentials and the static provider never contains it. Because the token appears in the request URI, treat signed URLs and any logs or error output that include the URI as secret-bearing material.

A token has no tracked expiry in this crate and is reused for the lifetime of the `Signer`. Replace the credential provider or create a new signer to use a different token. Query authentication has no separate presign lifetime here, so signing rejects `expires_in`.

The caller owns the API host, method, path, other query parameters, headers (including `User-Agent`), and request body. Do not forward a signed request to an unrelated host.

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

This provider has no ambient default source. Supply an explicit credential provider as described on this page.

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-baidu-netdisk/latest/reqsign%5Fbaidu%5Fnetdisk/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static access token

# Cloudflare | Apache Reqsign™

# Cloudflare

Cloudflare API v4 requests authenticated with an API token, including the Workers KV and D1 endpoints. The account, database, and namespace IDs stay in the caller-built request URL.

Bearer token✓ header signing— query / presign✓ WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-cloudflare ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-cloudflare)

Inserts a sensitive Authorization: Bearer header and leaves the URI and every other header unchanged; expires\_in is rejected because the Cloudflare API has no query authentication.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features cloudflare


```

```

use reqsign::{cloudflare, default_context};


// CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN — resolved by the default chain.

let ctx = default_context();

let signer = cloudflare::default_signer(ctx);


let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::GET)

    .uri("https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/<account_id>/storage/kv/namespaces/<namespace_id>/values/my-key")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

The signer inserts `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, which is how API tokens authenticate the Cloudflare API v4\. One token signs KV and D1 requests alike.

## Resource identifiers stay in the request[​](#resource-identifiers-stay-in-the-request "Direct link to Resource identifiers stay in the request")

The account, database, and namespace identifiers are part of the request URL rather than the credential:

```

KV   /accounts/<account_id>/storage/kv/namespaces/<namespace_id>/values/<key>

D1   /accounts/<account_id>/d1/database/<database_id>/query


```

They stay with the code that builds the request, so one credential signs for every account, database, and namespace the token is scoped to. Reqsign does not build the business URL, choose the HTTP method, or touch the request body: keep the multipart `Content-Type` for KV writes and the JSON body for D1 queries in the caller.

## Credential discovery[​](#credential-discovery "Direct link to Credential discovery")

The default chain reads `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` through `Context` environment access. That is the variable Wrangler and Cloudflare's official SDKs use for non-interactive authentication. There is no other default source.

Cloudflare's global API key is not an API token source: it authenticates with`X-Auth-Key` and `X-Auth-Email` instead of a bearer token, so`CLOUDFLARE_API_KEY` and `CLOUDFLARE_EMAIL` are not read. Supply a custom provider when a request really needs that authentication.

`CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` is not read either; it selects a resource in the URL, not an identity.

The configured sources fail closed. A present but unusable`CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, or an invalid prepended or static provider, fails signing instead of silently selecting a different identity. An absent token yields no credential, and signing then reports `CredentialInvalid`.

## Explicit credentials[​](#explicit-credentials "Direct link to Explicit credentials")

Replace the provider for a token managed by your application:

```

use reqsign::cloudflare::{StaticCredentialProvider, default_signer};


let ctx = reqsign::default_context();

let signer = default_signer(ctx)

    .with_credential_provider(StaticCredentialProvider::new("cloudflare-api-token"));


```

The builder exposes one positive method and one removal method per slot:

```

use reqsign::cloudflare::{DefaultCredentialProvider, EnvCredentialProvider};


let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::builder()

    .no_env()

    .env(EnvCredentialProvider::new())

    .build();


```

Removed slots are not re-enabled during `build()`. `push_front` composes a higher-priority provider, and an error from a prepended provider is returned instead of falling through to the default chain. A caller-supplied`ProvideCredentialChain` keeps that chain's own error policy.

## Request behavior[​](#request-behavior "Direct link to Request behavior")

`RequestSigner` inserts a sensitive `Authorization` header and leaves the URI and every other header unchanged. The Cloudflare API has no query authentication, so signing rejects `expires_in`.

Cloudflare assigns each token its permissions and optional expiry when the token is created; neither is readable from the token. Reqsign does not track that expiry, and signing writes no protocol time, so signing has no clock dependency. A token that Cloudflare has expired fails at the API, so rotate it with the mechanism your deployment already uses.

The caller owns the HTTP client and its redirect policy. Do not forward the signed `Authorization` header to a different host.

## WASM[​](#wasm "Direct link to WASM")

Environment and static credentials plus header signing work on`wasm32-unknown-unknown` without a JavaScript clock.

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

The default signer tries these sources in order and uses the first one that yields a credential — no configuration needed when any of them is present:

1. CLOUDFLARE\_API\_TOKEN

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [EnvCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-cloudflare/latest/reqsign%5Fcloudflare/struct.EnvCredentialProvider.html) — CLOUDFLARE\_API\_TOKEN
* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-cloudflare/latest/reqsign%5Fcloudflare/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static Cloudflare API token

# Dropbox | Apache Reqsign™

# Dropbox

Dropbox API requests authenticated with a Dropbox OAuth 2.0 access token.

OAuth 2.0 bearer token✓ header signing— query / presign✓ WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-dropbox ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-dropbox)

Inserts a sensitive Authorization: Bearer header; expires\_in is rejected because Dropbox has no query authentication.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features dropbox


```

```

use reqsign::{default_context, dropbox};


// The default chain reads DBXCLI_ACCESS_TOKEN through the context environment.

let ctx = default_context();

let signer = dropbox::default_signer(ctx);


let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::POST)

    .uri("https://api.dropboxapi.com/2/users/get_current_account")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

The default source is the `DBXCLI_ACCESS_TOKEN` variable documented by the official `dbxcli` tool. Reqsign does not read `dbxcli` account or team files. For an explicit access token, use `StaticCredentialProvider`; for long-lived access, replace the provider with `RefreshCredentialProvider`:

```

use reqsign::dropbox::{RefreshCredentialProvider, default_signer};


let ctx = reqsign::default_context();

let provider =

    RefreshCredentialProvider::new("client-id", "client-secret", "refresh-token")?;

let signer = default_signer(ctx).with_credential_provider(provider);


```

The refresh provider sends the client ID and secret in the RFC 6749 form body and uses Dropbox's fixed token endpoint unless the caller explicitly replaces it with another trusted HTTPS endpoint. It rejects a successful token response that omits `expires_in`, because Dropbox access tokens are expected to expire and an unknown lifetime must not be cached as permanent. The default source and prepended providers fail closed: a failed explicit refresh or an unusable explicit token returns an error instead of falling through to`DBXCLI_ACCESS_TOKEN`.

Dropbox uses header authentication only. Signing adds a sensitive`Authorization: Bearer` header and rejects `expires_in`; it never modifies the URI or other headers. Refresh-token rotation is serialized per shared provider, and the access-token cache belongs to `Signer`.

On `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, this provider enables Jiff's JavaScript clock. Runtime signing requires a wasm-bindgen JavaScript host such as a browser or Node; a bare WASM runtime without a JavaScript clock is not supported. CI exercises the public default signer path under `wasm-bindgen-test` in Node.

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

The default signer tries these sources in order and uses the first one that yields a credential — no configuration needed when any of them is present:

1. DBXCLI\_ACCESS\_TOKEN from the official dbxcli tool

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [EnvCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-dropbox/latest/reqsign%5Fdropbox/struct.EnvCredentialProvider.html) — DBXCLI\_ACCESS\_TOKEN from the official dbxcli tool
* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-dropbox/latest/reqsign%5Fdropbox/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static access token with optional absolute expiry
* [RefreshCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-dropbox/latest/reqsign%5Fdropbox/struct.RefreshCredentialProvider.html) — OAuth 2.0 refresh-token exchange

# GitHub | Apache Reqsign™

# GitHub

GitHub.com REST API requests at https://api.github.com, authenticated with a bearer token or sent anonymously for public resources.

Bearer token✓ header signing— query / presign✓ WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-github ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-github)

Inserts a sensitive Authorization: Bearer header for token credentials and removes any existing Authorization header for anonymous credentials; other headers and the URI are unchanged, and expires\_in is rejected.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features github


```

```

use reqsign::{default_context, github};


// GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN, then the GitHub CLI, then anonymous public access.

let ctx = default_context();

let signer = github::default_signer(ctx);


let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::GET)

    .uri("https://api.github.com/repos/apache/reqsign/contents/README.md")

    .header("user-agent", "my-application")

    .header("x-github-api-version", "2022-11-28")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

The default chain reads `GH_TOKEN` before `GITHUB_TOKEN`. If neither is set and the context has a `CommandExecute` adapter, it resolves the active stored account with `gh config get user --host github.com`, then reads that account's token with`gh auth token --hostname github.com --user <user> --no-refresh`. The explicit user prevents `GH_TOKEN` or `GITHUB_TOKEN` in the child process environment from shadowing the stored credential; safe stored-token discovery requires GitHub CLI 2.40.0 or newer. The commands run directly, never through a shell; the explicit host keeps discovery independent of `GH_HOST` and local Git remotes; and Reqsign does not parse the CLI's configuration files.

`--no-refresh` keeps discovery read-only on GitHub CLI 2.103.0 and newer. Older supported versions do not refresh when printing a stored token, so the provider retries without the flag only after the CLI reports that specific flag as unknown. If the stored token has expired, run `gh auth refresh`, then recreate the signer so it loads the new token.

The default slots stop at the first error instead of silently selecting a different identity. A malformed environment token, malformed or failed stored-token discovery, or an invalid prepended or static provider fails signing. Only an absent credential reaches anonymous access.

With no token, the chain ends with anonymous access. Signing with an anonymous credential removes any existing `Authorization` header and leaves other headers and the URI unchanged, so a reused request cannot carry stale authentication material. Anonymous requests can read public resources and are subject to GitHub's 60-requests-per-hour unauthenticated rate limit. Remove the fallback with `.no_anonymous()` when every request must be authenticated.

## Explicit credentials[​](#explicit-credentials "Direct link to Explicit credentials")

Replace the provider for a token managed by your application:

```

use reqsign::github::{StaticCredentialProvider, default_signer};


let ctx = reqsign::default_context();

let signer = default_signer(ctx)

    .with_credential_provider(StaticCredentialProvider::new("github-token"));


```

The builder exposes one positive method and one removal method per slot:

```

use reqsign::github::DefaultCredentialProvider;


let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::builder()

    .no_env()

    .no_gh_cli()

    .build();


```

Removed slots are not re-enabled during `build()`. `.env(provider)`,`.gh_cli(provider)`, and `.anonymous(provider)` replace a slot, while`push_front` and `with_chain` compose a provider in front of or instead of the default chain.

## Request behavior[​](#request-behavior "Direct link to Request behavior")

`RequestSigner` adds a sensitive `Authorization: Bearer` header for a token credential and removes any existing `Authorization` header for an explicit anonymous credential. Other headers and the URI are unchanged. It does not add or replace `User-Agent` (GitHub requires the caller to send one), `Accept`, or`X-GitHub-Api-Version`, so keep those request headers in the caller. GitHub has no query authentication, so signing rejects `expires_in`. GitHub credentials in this crate carry no expiration and signing writes no protocol time, so signing has no clock dependency.

## Host and scope[​](#host-and-scope "Direct link to Host and scope")

The built-in providers discover GitHub.com credentials only. They ignore`GH_HOST`, `GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN`; use`StaticCredentialProvider` or a custom provider for GitHub Enterprise Server.`GH_TOKEN` and `GITHUB_TOKEN` are interpreted as the GitHub CLI's GitHub.com token; pass the intended token explicitly when you use multiple hosts. The signer does not restrict the request host, so caller-supplied credentials may be used with another GitHub host. GitHub assigns each token's host and its OAuth scopes or fine-grained repository permissions. Reqsign neither requests nor inspects them, and it does not implement GitHub App installation-token exchange.

The caller owns the HTTP client and its redirect policy. Do not forward the signed `Authorization` header to a different host.

## WASM[​](#wasm "Direct link to WASM")

Environment, static, and anonymous signing work on `wasm32-unknown-unknown`without a JavaScript clock. GitHub CLI discovery requires a `CommandExecute`adapter and is unavailable in bare WASM runtimes.

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

The default signer tries these sources in order and uses the first one that yields a credential — no configuration needed when any of them is present:

1. GH\_TOKEN, then GITHUB\_TOKEN, for github.com
2. Stored GitHub.com token from gh config get user and gh auth token --user (gh 2.40+)
3. Anonymous public access

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [EnvCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-github/latest/reqsign%5Fgithub/struct.EnvCredentialProvider.html) — GH\_TOKEN, then GITHUB\_TOKEN, for github.com
* [GhCliCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-github/latest/reqsign%5Fgithub/struct.GhCliCredentialProvider.html) — Stored GitHub.com token from gh config get user and gh auth token --user (gh 2.40+)
* [AnonymousCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-github/latest/reqsign%5Fgithub/struct.AnonymousCredentialProvider.html) — Anonymous public access
* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-github/latest/reqsign%5Fgithub/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static GitHub token

# HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421) | Apache Reqsign™

# HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421)

HTTP APIs that accept RFC 9421 request signatures, with the caller choosing the signature label, covered components, and an HMAC-SHA256 or RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 SHA-256 credential.

RFC 9421 HMAC-SHA256RFC 9421 RSASSA-PKCS1-v1\_5 SHA-256✓ header signing— query / presign✓ WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-http-message-signatures ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-http-message-signatures)

Adds Signature-Input and Signature request headers. The caller supplies any Content-Digest. expires\_in adds a checked expires parameter; it does not select query authentication.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features http-message-signatures


```

RFC 9421 leaves the signature label and covered components to the application, so there is no default signer. Assemble the policy explicitly:

```

use http::header::HeaderName;

use reqsign::http_message_signatures::{

    Component, Credential, RequestSigner, StaticCredentialProvider,

};

use reqsign::{Signer, default_context};


let ctx = default_context();

let request_signer = RequestSigner::new(

    "sig1",

    [

        Component::Method,

        Component::Authority,

        Component::Path,

        Component::Header(HeaderName::from_static("content-digest")),

    ],

)?;

let signer = Signer::new(

    ctx,

    StaticCredentialProvider::new(Credential::hmac_sha256("my-key", b"shared secret")?),

    request_signer,

);


let mut parts = http::Request::builder()

    .method("POST")

    .uri("https://example.com/upload?part=1")

    .header("content-digest", "sha-256=:...:")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


signer.sign(&mut parts, None).await?;


```

## Scope[​](#scope "Direct link to Scope")

This first version signs request heads with HMAC-SHA256 or RSASSA-PKCS1-v1\_5 SHA-256\. It supports ordinary request fields and the`@method`, `@target-uri`, `@authority`, `@scheme`, `@path`, and `@query`derived components. Percent escapes, query order, and repeated query parameters are preserved.

The signer requires an absolute HTTP or HTTPS URI. `@target-uri` is rebuilt from the scheme, the authority exactly as written, and the origin-form path/query, with an empty path normalized to `/`. A present `Host` header must be unique and byte-identical to the URI authority; case-only or explicit/default-port differences are rejected because an HTTP/1.1 origin-form receiver could reconstruct a different target URI. Origin-form request targets without an absolute URI are not supported.

Verification, response signing, multiple signatures in one call, component parameters, `@request-target`, and body I/O are out of scope. To cover a body, compute a `Content-Digest` before signing and include it in the component list.

HMAC uses raw shared-key bytes. RSA accepts unencrypted PKCS#1 or PKCS#8 PEM and uses the context's `CryptoProvider`. The RustCrypto provider supports RSA on native targets but returns `ConfigInvalid` for it on `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. The HMAC path runs on `wasm32-unknown-unknown` when hosted by a JavaScript runtime through wasm-bindgen, such as a browser or Node. Jiff reads the clock from that host; a bare WASM runtime without a JavaScript clock is unsupported.

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

The default signer tries these sources in order and uses the first one that yields a credential — no configuration needed when any of them is present:

1. Caller-supplied HMAC or RSA credential

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-http-message-signatures/latest/reqsign%5Fhttp%5Fmessage%5Fsignatures/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Caller-supplied HMAC or RSA credential

url: https://reqsign.apache.org/docs/providers/huaweicloud-obs/

# Huawei Cloud OBS | Apache Reqsign™

# Huawei Cloud OBS

Huawei Cloud Object Storage Service requests signed with the OBS signature.

OBS signature✓ header signing✓ query / presign— WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-huaweicloud-obs ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-huaweicloud-obs)

expires\_in selects query authentication with AccessKeyId, Expires, and Signature parameters.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features huaweicloud


```

```

use reqsign::{default_context, huaweicloud};


// Environment credentials — resolved by the default chain.

let ctx = default_context();

let signer = huaweicloud::default_signer(ctx, "my-bucket");


let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::GET)

    .uri("https://my-bucket.obs.cn-north-4.myhuaweicloud.com/my-object")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

## Credential expiry[​](#credential-expiry "Direct link to Credential expiry")

`Credential` has an absolute `expires_at: Option<Timestamp>` field.`Credential::new` keeps its original three-argument, no-expiry behavior; use`Credential::with_expires_at` when the expiration is known. The added public field means existing struct-literal construction no longer compiles, so struct-literal callers must switch to `Credential::new` (and`with_expires_at` where needed).

`AgencyGrant` and `AgencyGranter` issue Huawei Cloud IAM agency temporary credentials through `Granter<Credential>`. The result carries the exact IAM`expires_at` and can be passed directly to `RequestSigner`. Known-expiry credentials are rejected by header signing or presigning when they do not cover the requested operation deadline.

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

The default signer tries these sources in order and uses the first one that yields a credential — no configuration needed when any of them is present:

1. Environment variables

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [EnvCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-huaweicloud-obs/latest/reqsign%5Fhuaweicloud%5Fobs/struct.EnvCredentialProvider.html) — Environment variables
* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-huaweicloud-obs/latest/reqsign%5Fhuaweicloud%5Fobs/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static access keys
* [ConfigCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-huaweicloud-obs/latest/reqsign%5Fhuaweicloud%5Fobs/struct.ConfigCredentialProvider.html) — Config-based credentials

# Koofr | Apache Reqsign™

# Koofr

Koofr API requests authenticated with a Koofr access token; mount selection, paths, and business requests remain caller-owned.

Koofr token authentication✓ header signing— query / presign✓ WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-koofr ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-koofr)

Adds a sensitive Authorization: Token token=<token> header; expires\_in is ignored because the documented exchange returns no expiry.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features koofr


```

```

use reqsign::{default_context, koofr};


// Pass the account email and an application-specific password explicitly.

let ctx = default_context();

let signer = koofr::default_signer(ctx, "me@example.com", "application-password");


let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::GET)

    .uri("https://app.koofr.net/api/v2/mounts/primary/files/list?path=%2F")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

The signer adds a sensitive `Authorization: Token token=<token>` header and leaves the URI unchanged.

## Credentials[​](#credentials "Direct link to Credentials")

`LoginCredentialProvider` exchanges an account email and an application-specific password at `POST https://app.koofr.net/token` with a JSON body:

```

{"email":"me@example.com","password":"application-password"}


```

A successful response is `{"token":"..."}`. The `/token` JSON exchange follows Koofr's first-party Go SDK; OpenDAL's Koofr backend uses the same exchange. Koofr's API Swagger documents Bearer and app-password Basic schemes separately, not this exchange. Generate the application-specific password at the[Koofr application preferences](https://app.koofr.net/app/admin/preferences/password); do not use the account login password.

Use `LoginCredentialProvider::with_endpoint` for a Koofr-compatible API endpoint. The endpoint must be an absolute HTTP(S) URI with a host, optional port, and optional path prefix. Userinfo, query strings, fragments, dot segments, backslashes, whitespace, and control characters are rejected. An explicit`http://` endpoint sends the email and application password in cleartext. Reqsign sends the exchange to the configured destination; redirect policy belongs to the configured `HttpSend` adapter.

`StaticCredentialProvider` accepts a token that the caller already holds. Koofr's first-party SDKs do not define a production environment-variable credential convention, so Reqsign does not discover ambient Koofr credentials. Mount selection, paths, and business requests stay with the caller.

The exchange does not return an expiry. The token stays cached until the caller replaces the `Signer` or installs a provider/context that starts a new cache. Koofr rejecting the token does not invalidate the cache automatically; the caller must replace the signer or its credential cache.

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

This provider has no ambient default source. Supply an explicit credential provider as described on this page.

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [LoginCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-koofr/latest/reqsign%5Fkoofr/struct.LoginCredentialProvider.html) — Email and application-specific password exchange
* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-koofr/latest/reqsign%5Fkoofr/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static access token

# OneDrive | Apache Reqsign™

# OneDrive

OneDrive and Microsoft Graph drive requests authenticated with a Microsoft Entra access token.

OAuth 2.0 bearer token✓ header signing— query / presign✓ WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-onedrive ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-onedrive)

Inserts a sensitive Authorization: Bearer header; expires\_in is rejected because this crate implements header authentication only.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features onedrive


```

OneDrive requests go to Microsoft Graph with a Microsoft Entra access token in an `Authorization: Bearer` header. Reqsign signs the request head; the caller builds the Graph request, for example`GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/me/drive/root`.

```

use reqsign::{default_context, onedrive::default_signer};

use reqsign::onedrive::{DefaultCredentialProvider, StaticCredentialProvider};


let ctx = default_context();

let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::new()

    .push_front(StaticCredentialProvider::new("graph-access-token"));

let signer = default_signer(ctx).with_credential_provider(provider);


let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::GET)

    .uri("https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/me/drive")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

Microsoft documents no environment variable or shared configuration file that carries a Microsoft Graph user token, and MSAL token caches are library-specific. `default_signer(ctx)` therefore composes a default provider whose automatic chain is empty: it does not run the Azure CLI, read MSAL caches, or start a login flow. Configure one source before signing:

* the documented refresh exchange, composed with`DefaultCredentialProvider::new().push_front(RefreshCredentialProvider::new(..)?)`
* a static access token or a custom provider, also composed with `push_front`; the provider pushed last is tried first

Supplying a provider directly to `Signer::new` or`Signer::with_credential_provider` is equivalent when you do not need the default chain.

## Refresh tokens[​](#refresh-tokens "Direct link to Refresh tokens")

The authorization request must include `offline_access` to receive a refresh token, plus the Microsoft Graph scope your access needs. `Files.ReadWrite` is the least privileged delegated permission that lets the app read, create, update, and delete the signed-in user's files, and `Files.Read` is the read-only alternative. Reqsign refreshes through`https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/v2.0/token`.

A **public client** — desktop, mobile, browserless, or client-side app — cannot store an application secret, so the exchange sends none:

```

use reqsign::{default_context, onedrive::default_signer};

use reqsign::onedrive::{DefaultCredentialProvider, RefreshCredentialProvider};


let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::new()

    .push_front(RefreshCredentialProvider::new("client-id", "refresh-token")?);

let signer = default_signer(default_context()).with_credential_provider(provider);


```

A **confidential client** — web app, web API, or daemon that keeps the secret on the server side — adds it to the same form-body exchange:

```

use reqsign::{default_context, onedrive::default_signer};

use reqsign::onedrive::{DefaultCredentialProvider, RefreshCredentialProvider};


let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::new().push_front(

    RefreshCredentialProvider::builder("client-id", "refresh-token")

        .client_secret("client-secret")

        .build()?,

);

let signer = default_signer(default_context()).with_credential_provider(provider);


```

Microsoft returns a new refresh token with every successful exchange and documents that the client must discard the previous one. A provider keeps only the latest refresh token in memory, clones share it, and exchanges are serialized, so concurrent signing never races two exchanges with the same token. Reqsign never writes refresh tokens to disk; a refresh token lost with the process must be obtained again through the authorization flow.

A Microsoft Graph token response carries `expires_in`. A successful exchange that omits it, or whose token is already expired, is rejected rather than cached as a token with an unknown lifetime; the returned refresh token from that response is still committed for the next exchange. Access-token caching and proactive refresh belong to `Signer`.

## Tenant, scope, and endpoint[​](#tenant-scope-and-endpoint "Direct link to Tenant, scope, and endpoint")

The default token endpoint is the global Microsoft Entra v2.0 endpoint for the`common` tenant. Microsoft documents `common`, `organizations`, `consumers`, or a tenant identifier such as a domain name or GUID; select one with `.tenant`:

```

use reqsign::onedrive::RefreshCredentialProvider;


let provider = RefreshCredentialProvider::builder("client-id", "refresh-token")

    .tenant("contoso.onmicrosoft.com")

    .build()?;


```

By default the exchange omits `scope`, which keeps the new access token limited to what the original grant received. To repeat the scope explicitly, use`.scope("offline_access Files.ReadWrite")`; Microsoft requires the value to be equivalent to or a subset of the original grant. Requesting a broader scope than the user consented to fails the exchange.

National clouds publish their own Microsoft Entra authentication endpoints, for example `https://login.microsoftonline.us` for Microsoft Entra ID for US Government and `https://login.partner.microsoftonline.cn` for Microsoft Entra China. Replace the whole endpoint in those clouds; it must be HTTPS:

```

use reqsign::onedrive::RefreshCredentialProvider;


let provider = RefreshCredentialProvider::builder("client-id", "refresh-token")

    .token_endpoint("https://login.microsoftonline.us/common/oauth2/v2.0/token")

    .build()?;


```

## Request authentication[​](#request-authentication "Direct link to Request authentication")

OneDrive uses header authentication only. Signing adds a sensitive`Authorization: Bearer` header and rejects `expires_in`, because this crate does not implement query authentication; it never modifies the URI or other headers. Business headers and parameters such as `$select`, `If-Match`, or the Graph drive path stay with the caller.

On `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, this provider enables Jiff's JavaScript clock. Runtime signing or refresh requires a wasm-bindgen JavaScript host such as a browser or Node; a bare WASM runtime without a JavaScript clock is not supported. CI exercises the public signing and refresh paths under`wasm-bindgen-test` in Node.

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

This provider has no ambient default source. Supply an explicit credential provider as described on this page.

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-onedrive/latest/reqsign%5Fonedrive/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static Microsoft Graph access token with optional absolute expiry
* [RefreshCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-onedrive/latest/reqsign%5Fonedrive/struct.RefreshCredentialProvider.html) — Microsoft Entra refresh-token exchange for a public or confidential client

# OpenStack Keystone | Apache Reqsign™

# OpenStack Keystone

OpenStack services that authenticate with a Keystone v3 token, such as Swift, including TempURL presigning.

X-Auth-Token headerSwift TempURL (HMAC-SHA1/256/512)✓ header signing✓ query / presign— WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-openstack-keystone ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-openstack-keystone)

Header signing inserts X-Auth-Token. TempURL presigning signs the method, expiry, and decoded object path with a separate account or container key, then appends temp\_url\_sig and temp\_url\_expires.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features openstack


```

```

use reqsign::{default_context, openstack};


// Environment variables — resolved by the default chain.

let ctx = default_context();

let signer = openstack::default_signer(ctx);


let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::GET)

    .uri("https://swift.example.com/v1/AUTH_test/container/object")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

The default chain uses a non-empty `OS_AUTH_TOKEN` as a pre-issued token and makes no Keystone request. When it is set, `OS_AUTH_URL`, `OS_USERNAME`, and`OS_PASSWORD` are not required, and an empty `OS_AUTH_TOKEN` is ignored. Without`OS_AUTH_TOKEN`, the chain authenticates against the Keystone v3 identity API with `OS_AUTH_URL`, `OS_USERNAME`, and `OS_PASSWORD`. A scoped token also carries the service catalog Keystone returned for it, so`Credential::endpoint_in_region` resolves the endpoint of a service such as Swift without another request.

A pre-issued token has no service catalog. When `OS_STORAGE_URL` is also set, the environment provider exposes it as the public `object-store` endpoint; otherwise the endpoint remains caller configuration. `StaticCredentialProvider`accepts an explicit token and optional catalog metadata. Install it directly or prepend it with `DefaultCredentialProvider::push_front`, and use`DefaultCredentialProvider::builder().no_env()` to remove both environment sources together.

## Swift TempURL[​](#swift-tempurl "Direct link to Swift TempURL")

TempURL presigning is separate from `X-Auth-Token` request signing. It uses the account or container key configured through `X-Account-Meta-Temp-URL-Key` or`X-Container-Meta-Temp-URL-Key`; it never uses a Keystone identity token as the key.

```

use std::time::Duration;


use reqsign::{default_context, openstack};


let ctx = default_context();

let signer = openstack::TempUrlSigner::new("account-tempurl-key")

    .with_algorithm(openstack::TempUrlHashAlgorithm::Sha256);

let uri = "https://swift.example.com/v1/AUTH_test/container/object"

    .parse()?;

let presigned = signer.presign(

    &ctx,

    &http::Method::GET,

    &uri,

    Duration::from_secs(3600),

)?;


```

The signature covers the method, the absolute expiration time, and the object path after decoding its percent escapes once, matching Swift's decoded request path. The outgoing URI keeps the caller's encoded path and query bytes and order. Existing non-auth query parameters are preserved, and a pre-existing TempURL authentication parameter is rejected even when its name is percent-encoded.

The provider always emits `sha1:`, `sha256:`, or `sha512:` HMAC tags with standard Base64 digests; SHA-256 is the default. Current Swift accepts this form, and the selected digest must be in the deployment's`tempurl.allowed_digests`. Current middleware defaults to all three, with SHA-1 deprecated, and deployments may restrict the list. A capability that exposes`tempurl` without `allowed_digests` belongs to the legacy raw-hex-only boundary, such as Swift 2.16, and is not supported even with SHA-1 selected. SHA-512 requires a `CryptoProvider` that implements `hmac_sha512`. Prefix-based and IP-restricted TempURLs are not provided.

Swift rebuilds the downstream query string from its recognized TempURL fields and removes or filters incoming headers according to the deployment configuration. This client preserves the caller's outgoing query and headers, but arbitrary query components or headers are not guaranteed to reach the storage service through a TempURL.

# Oracle Cloud | Apache Reqsign™

# Oracle Cloud

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure services authenticating with the OCI HTTP request signature.

OCI request signature✓ header signing— query / presign— WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-oracle ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-oracle)

Header signing only; expires\_in is not interpreted as query authentication.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features oracle


```

```

use reqsign::{default_context, oracle};


// Env and the OCI config file (~/.oci/config) — resolved by the default chain.

let ctx = default_context();

let signer = oracle::default_signer(ctx);


let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::GET)

    .uri("https://objectstorage.us-ashburn-1.oraclecloud.com/n/my-namespace/b/my-bucket/o/my-object")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

## Request body headers[​](#request-body-headers "Direct link to Request body headers")

For `POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH` requests, OCI requires `content-length`,`content-type`, and `x-content-sha256` in the signature. Set these headers on the request before calling `sign`; reqsign signs the supplied values and does not read the body. `x-content-sha256` is the base64-encoded SHA-256 digest of the body; for an empty body it is`47DEQpj8HBSa+/TImW+5JCeuQeRkm5NMpJWZG3hSuFU=`. Set the headers before signing; headers added or replaced by the HTTP client afterwards are not covered by the signature.

Object Storage `PutObject` and `UploadPart` PUT requests may omit the body headers. If they are present, reqsign signs them. `GET`, `HEAD`, and `DELETE`requests keep signing only `date`, `(request-target)`, and `host`.

### Default credential chain

* [EnvCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-oracle/latest/reqsign%5Foracle/struct.EnvCredentialProvider.html) — Environment variables
* [ConfigFileCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-oracle/latest/reqsign%5Foracle/struct.ConfigFileCredentialProvider.html) — OCI config file (\~/.oci/config)
* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-oracle/latest/reqsign%5Foracle/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static API key material

# Seafile | Apache Reqsign™

# Seafile

Self-hosted Seafile Web API requests authenticated with an account token or repository API token.

Authorization: Token header✓ header signing— query / presign✓ WASM[docs.rs/reqsign-seafile ↗](https://docs.rs/reqsign-seafile)

Inserts a sensitive Authorization: Token header. Configuration-discovered and account-exchange credentials are bound to the deployment scheme, host, effective port, and base path; static credentials remain caller-scoped. Seafile has no query authentication, so expires\_in is rejected.

## Get started[​](#get-started "Direct link to Get started")

```

cargo add reqsign --features seafile


```

```

use reqsign::{default_context, seafile};


// Reads the [account] server and token from ~/.seafile.conf.

let ctx = default_context();

let signer = seafile::default_signer(ctx);


let mut req = http::Request::builder()

    .method(http::Method::GET)

    .uri("https://files.example.com/api2/repos/")

    .body(())?

    .into_parts()

    .0;


// Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use.

signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;


```

The default chain reads `server` and `token` from the `[account]` section of`~/.seafile.conf`, the user configuration file read by Seafile's first-party`seaf-cli`, and binds the credential to that deployment. The `server` value is required. `ConfigFileCredentialProvider::with_account_user` can require the`[account] user` value to match an explicitly selected account. Duplicate`[account]` sections or repeated parsed keys are rejected. Seafile does not document a standard credential environment variable or login command, so the default chain does not invent one.

## Account token exchange[​](#account-token-exchange "Direct link to Account token exchange")

Use `AccountTokenCredentialProvider` when the caller has a username and password and wants Reqsign to obtain the account token:

```

use reqsign::{Context, Signer};

use reqsign_http_send_reqwest::ReqwestHttpSend;

use reqsign_seafile::{AccountTokenCredentialProvider, RequestSigner};

use reqwest::redirect::Policy;


let client = reqwest::Client::builder()

    .redirect(Policy::none())

    .build()

    .expect("client must build");

let ctx = Context::new().with_http_send(ReqwestHttpSend::new(client));

let signer = Signer::new(

    ctx,

    AccountTokenCredentialProvider::new(

        "https://files.example.com/seafile",

        "user@example.com",

        "password",

    ),

    RequestSigner,

);


```

This example needs direct dependencies on `reqsign` (with the `seafile`feature), `reqsign-http-send-reqwest`, `reqsign-seafile`, and `reqwest`.

The provider posts form-encoded `username` and `password` fields to`{server}/api2/auth-token/` and reads the `token` field from the JSON response. The current OpenAPI document describes a JSON request body, but Seafile's server-side example, `seaf-cli`, and the Python SDK post form fields; this crate follows those executable clients. The `server` value may include a reverse-proxy base path, which is preserved.

The provider constructs only the initial request to the configured server. The`HttpSend` adapter owns redirect policy: `ReqwestHttpSend::default()` follows redirects, so the credential-bearing exchange should use a client with redirects disabled as shown above. Use HTTPS in production; an explicit `http://` endpoint sends the login secret in cleartext. Two-factor authentication is not part of this exchange, so use a token obtained separately when the server requires it.

## Scope and compatibility[​](#scope-and-compatibility "Direct link to Scope and compatibility")

`RequestSigner` adds a sensitive `Authorization: Token <token>` header and leaves the URI and other headers unchanged. Seafile 11 and newer also accept `Bearer`, but `Token` works with older self-hosted servers and matches existing OpenDAL behavior. Seafile has no query authentication, so `expires_in` is rejected.

Credentials discovered from `seaf-cli` configuration or obtained through the account exchange are bound to the deployment that supplied them. Before adding the header, the signer checks the request scheme, host, effective port, and deployment base path on a segment boundary. A `/seafile` deployment accepts`/seafile` and `/seafile/...` but not `/seafile-other`; a mismatch fails without changing the request. Scoped signing also rejects a duplicate or conflicting`Host` header and ambiguous path forms that the HTTP adapter would normalize. Static caller-supplied credentials carry no deployment scope and keep the explicit caller contract. Credential caching preserves the deployment, so every signing call rechecks it.

Repository id discovery, repository-scoped upload and download links, and business request construction remain with the caller. Account and repository API tokens have no documented expiration; `Signer` caches the token until the signer is recreated or its provider is replaced. Redirect policy after signing remains the caller's adapter responsibility.

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

The default signer tries these sources in order and uses the first one that yields a credential — no configuration needed when any of them is present:

1. Seafile CLI user configuration (\~/.seafile.conf)

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [ConfigFileCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-seafile/latest/reqsign%5Fseafile/struct.ConfigFileCredentialProvider.html) — Seafile CLI user configuration (\~/.seafile.conf)
* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-seafile/latest/reqsign%5Fseafile/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static account or repository API token
* [AccountTokenCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-seafile/latest/reqsign%5Fseafile/struct.AccountTokenCredentialProvider.html) — Configured username and password exchange

# Tencent COS | Apache Reqsign™

## Credentials

### Default credential chain

The default signer tries these sources in order and uses the first one that yields a credential — no configuration needed when any of them is present:

1. Environment variables
2. STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity (OIDC)

### Credential providers

Available `ProvideCredential` implementations. Construct any of them directly, reorder them, or compose them into your own chain — see [Loading credentials](/docs/guides/credentials/):

* [EnvCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-tencent-cos/latest/reqsign%5Ftencent%5Fcos/struct.EnvCredentialProvider.html) — Environment variables
* [AssumeRoleWithWebIdentityCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-tencent-cos/latest/reqsign%5Ftencent%5Fcos/struct.AssumeRoleWithWebIdentityCredentialProvider.html) — STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity (OIDC)
* [StaticCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-tencent-cos/latest/reqsign%5Ftencent%5Fcos/struct.StaticCredentialProvider.html) — Static access keys
* [ConfigCredentialProvider](https://docs.rs/reqsign-tencent-cos/latest/reqsign%5Ftencent%5Fcos/struct.ConfigCredentialProvider.html) — Config-based credentials

url: https://reqsign.apache.org/docs/providers/upyun/
